content: Key populations at ongoing risk for HIV should be prioritized for testing services, as outlined in Chapter 5. HIV testing services (HTS) in specific health facilities can target populations or areas with high HIV prevalence or unmet testing needs. These services can also focus on high-risk groups, such as sexual and social networks with ongoing HIV transmission risk, partners, family members, peers, or social contacts of people living with HIV. Other vulnerable groups, such as men, adolescents in high-burden settings, and migrant workers, may also benefit from targeted testing depending on the local context. Chapter 6 provides further considerations for specific populations. HTS can also be geographically focused, targeting districts or areas with high HIV burden and ongoing transmission, such as transport hubs, border crossings, or urban locales where key populations work or reside. Community-based testing, mobile outreach, and home-based testing in areas with low testing coverage and high HIV prevalence or incidence are effective strategies. Geographic prioritization can help scale up new HTS approaches gradually as resources become available. Indicator condition-guided HTS involves offering testing to individuals presenting with clinical conditions indicative of HIV, such as cervical or anal cancer, herpes zoster, or unexplained fever. This approach has been successfully implemented in routine healthcare settings in Europe, supported by WHO guidance. Data from 20 low HIV-burden European countries showed a 3% HIV positivity rate when testing was offered to individuals with indicator conditions. Partner services, including voluntary provider-assisted referral, should be offered to all people living with HIV to reach their sexual or drug-injecting partners and biological children with unknown HIV status. Strategic planning for effective HTS delivery, as discussed in Chapter 7, requires staff training and may involve providing an abbreviated list of indicator conditions specific to the setting. HIV testing should also be integrated into services for individuals with tuberculosis (TB), sexually transmitted infections (STIs), or viral hepatitis, as these settings are effective in identifying HIV infections. Risk-based screening tools or questionnaires can help identify individuals who would benefit from HTS in settings where testing is not routinely offered. For example, in Nigeria, introducing a validated screening tool increased HTS coverage among sick and hospitalized children by 27% and newly diagnosed HIV cases by 36%. Retesting is essential for individuals with ongoing HIV-related risk, such as key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals) and those with known HIV-positive partners who are not virally suppressed. WHO recommends annual retesting for sexually active individuals in high-burden settings and those with ongoing risk. Pregnant and breastfeeding women face an increased risk of HIV acquisition, particularly in high-burden settings or if they have partners with HIV. All pregnant women should be offered testing for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B as early as possible during pregnancy, ideally at the first antenatal care visit. In high-burden settings, retesting in the third trimester is advised for women with unknown or HIV-negative status. Additional postpartum testing may be considered for women from key populations or those with HIV-positive partners who are not virally suppressed. Mathematical modeling and cost-effectiveness analyses indicate that maternal HIV retesting during pregnancy is cost-effective in high-burden countries like Kenya and South Africa but not in low-burden countries like Colombia or Ukraine. Dual HIV/syphilis testing at the first antenatal visit is cost-saving in both highand low-burden settings. Retesting individuals with HIV who are not on antiretroviral therapy (ART) or receiving other HIV care can help re-engage them in care. This includes those diagnosed in the pre-ART era or those who disengaged from care after starting ART. Efforts should focus on effective linkage to ART for these individuals. Conducting in-depth situational analyses is critical for optimizing HTS delivery. This involves reviewing data disaggregated by sex, age, population type, geography, and HTS approach to identify service delivery gaps and prioritize testing efforts. Cost considerations for HTS programs include direct medical costs (e.g., personnel, test kits), non-medical costs (e.g., transportation, incentives), and costs incurred by test recipients (e.g., travel expenses, time off work). Programs should evaluate the cost-effectiveness of different HTS approaches and consider the incremental costs of introducing new strategies. For example, provider-assisted referral may be costly to implement but efficient in identifying undiagnosed HIV cases, potentially lowering the cost per positive diagnosis.
